headline: Urgent: sensitive files are publicly exposed.

industry.label: Real estate
industry.note: Real estate is a top target for wire-fraud email scams: criminals pose as an agent or title company to redirect closing funds. Strong SPF, DKIM and DMARC (set to p=reject) make it much harder for anyone to send convincing fake emails in your name, which protects your clients and your reputation.

priorities.title: Sensitive files exposed
priorities.why: Anyone can download /.git/HEAD (part of your source-code history (.git), which can let anyone download your site's code).

priorities.title: DKIM (email signatures)
priorities.why: Your email runs on Google Workspace, but DKIM signing isn't turned on, so receivers can't verify your messages are really from you.

priorities.title: DMARC (email spoofing policy)
priorities.why: You have DMARC, but it's set to p=none: fake emails are reported but still delivered.

checks.title: HTTPS encryption
checks.detail: Your site loads over HTTPS, so information visitors send is encrypted.

checks.title: HTTP to HTTPS redirect
checks.detail: Visitors who type http:// are sent to the secure https:// version.

checks.title: HSTS (always use HTTPS)
checks.detail: HSTS is on, but only for 1 day, which is shorter than recommended.
checks.fix: Raise it to at least six months: max-age=31536000. On WordPress you can add it to the .htaccess file in your site's main folder (ask your host if you're unsure), or use a headers plugin.

snippets.label: Apache / LiteSpeed (.htaccess)
snippets.code:
<IfModule mod_headers.c>
  Header always set Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains"
</IfModule>

checks.title: Certificate expiry
checks.detail: Your certificate is valid until 2027-01-01 (44 days).

checks.title: Content Security Policy
checks.detail: There's no Content Security Policy, so if an attacker manages to inject code into a page, browsers will run it.
checks.fix: Add a Content Security Policy. Start in report-only mode (below) so nothing breaks, check your browser console for a week, then rename the header to Content-Security-Policy. On WordPress, plugins often need extra sources added; a developer should tune it.

snippets.label: Apache / LiteSpeed (.htaccess)
snippets.code:
<IfModule mod_headers.c>
  Header always set Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only "default-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'"
</IfModule>

checks.title: Clickjacking protection
checks.detail: Other websites can load your pages inside a hidden frame and trick visitors into clicking buttons (clickjacking).
checks.fix: Add the header X-Frame-Options: DENY (or SAMEORIGIN), or frame-ancestors 'none' in your CSP. On WordPress you can add it to the .htaccess file in your site's main folder (ask your host if you're unsure), or use a headers plugin.

checks.title: MIME-sniffing protection
checks.detail: Browsers are told not to guess file types, which closes a class of upload and script tricks.

checks.title: Referrer policy
checks.detail: Without a referrer policy, the full address of your pages (which can include private details) may be sent to other sites.
checks.fix: Add the header Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin. On WordPress you can add it to the .htaccess file in your site's main folder (ask your host if you're unsure), or use a headers plugin.

checks.title: Permissions policy
checks.detail: There's no permissions policy, so any script on your site could ask for the camera, microphone or location.
checks.fix: Add a Permissions-Policy header, for example: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(). On WordPress you can add it to the .htaccess file in your site's main folder (ask your host if you're unsure), or use a headers plugin.

snippets.label: Apache / LiteSpeed (.htaccess)
snippets.code:
<IfModule mod_headers.c>
  Header always set Permissions-Policy "camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()"
</IfModule>

checks.title: Software version hidden
checks.detail: Your server announces its software and version (Server: Apache/2.4.41 (Ubuntu)). That helps attackers look up known weaknesses.
checks.fix: Turn off version banners (for example server_tokens off in nginx, ServerTokens Prod in Apache, expose_php = Off in PHP). Many shared hosts control this; ask them to hide the Server version and set expose_php = Off.

checks.title: Outdated software
checks.detail: jquery 1.12.4 has 2 known security issues; WordPress 6.1.1 is out of date (the latest is 6.8.1); PHP 7.4 stopped getting security fixes on 2022-11-28. Attackers scan the internet for exactly these versions and use published exploits against them.
checks.fix: In WordPress, go to Dashboard → Updates and update WordPress, then all plugins and themes. Turn on automatic updates for plugins you trust, and delete plugins and themes you don't use. Take a backup first.

checks.title: Cookie security
checks.detail: Some cookies aren't fully protected: PHPSESSID (missing Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite). Unprotected cookies can be stolen over insecure connections or by injected scripts, letting someone take over a logged-in session.
checks.fix: Mark cookies Secure and SameSite=Lax, and mark login/session cookies HttpOnly.

checks.title: Mixed content
checks.detail: Your secure page loads 1 item(s) over insecure http://, for example http://smithrealty.com/wp-content/uploads/logo.png. Browsers block or warn about these, and they can be tampered with.
checks.fix: Update the old http:// links to https://. On WordPress, a search-and-replace plugin (back up first) or an SSL plugin can do this across your whole site.

checks.title: Secure forms
checks.detail: 1 form(s) on your home page send information to an insecure http:// address, so anything visitors type (names, emails, maybe more) travels unencrypted.
checks.fix: Change each form's action address to https://, or have your developer fix the form plugin.

checks.title: Third-party scripts
checks.detail: Your home page runs code from 2 outside service(s): www.googletagmanager.com, connect.facebook.net. Each one can change what runs on your site, so if any is hacked, your visitors are affected.
checks.fix: Remove scripts you no longer use. For fixed-version libraries loaded from a CDN, add Subresource Integrity (integrity="sha384-...") so tampered files are blocked.

checks.title: SPF (email sender list)
checks.detail: Your SPF record tells email providers which servers may send email for your domain.

checks.title: DKIM (email signatures)
checks.detail: Your email runs on Google Workspace, but DKIM signing isn't turned on, so receivers can't verify your messages are really from you.
checks.fix: In the Google Admin console: Apps → Google Workspace → Gmail → Authenticate email. Generate a DKIM key, add the TXT record it gives you, then click Start authentication.

checks.title: DMARC (email spoofing policy)
checks.detail: You have DMARC, but it's set to p=none: fake emails are reported but still delivered.
checks.fix: Once your reports show your real email passes, change it to p=quarantine, then p=reject.

checks.title: MTA-STS (encrypted email delivery)
checks.detail: Optional: you don't publish MTA-STS, which forces other mail servers to encrypt email they deliver to you.
checks.fix: Once SPF, DKIM and DMARC are solid, consider MTA-STS (your email provider has a guide).

checks.title: Domain renewal
checks.detail: smithrealty.com expires in 39 days (2026-12-27).
checks.fix: Make sure auto-renew is on and your payment card is current.

checks.title: Domain transfer lock
checks.detail: Your domain isn't transfer-locked, which makes it easier to hijack if your registrar account is compromised.
checks.fix: Turn on "Domain lock" / "Transfer lock" at your registrar, and protect that account with two-factor login.

checks.title: DNSSEC (tamper-proof DNS)
checks.detail: DNSSEC isn't turned on, so in some attacks your visitors or email could be quietly redirected to a fake server.
checks.fix: Turn on DNSSEC at your DNS provider, then add the DS record at your domain registrar (often one click if they're the same company).

checks.title: CAA (who may issue certificates)
checks.detail: Optional: smithrealty.com has no CAA record, so any certificate authority may issue a certificate for it.
checks.fix: Add a CAA record naming the certificate authority your host uses (for example letsencrypt.org).

snippets.label: DNS record (adjust to the certificate authority your host uses)

checks.title: Sensitive files exposed
checks.detail: Anyone can download /.git/HEAD (part of your source-code history (.git), which can let anyone download your site's code).
checks.fix: Remove these files from your web server or block access to them today. Then change any passwords or keys they contained, and assume they have already been copied.

checks.title: security.txt contact
checks.detail: Optional: you don't publish a security.txt file telling researchers how to report problems.
checks.fix: Add /.well-known/security.txt with a Contact: line (see securitytxt.org).

disclaimer: This free check only looks at public information, the same way a browser or email provider does, plus public records (domain registration, certificate logs and vulnerability databases). It can't see inside your site, logins, plugins or server, so it isn't a full security audit.
